A friend of mine in the East once wrote to me and asked me to visit an old man named Simon Wheeler. <break time="0.8s" /> He wanted me to ask Wheeler about his childhood friend, the Reverend Leonidas W, Smiley. <break time="0.8s" /> Later I began to suspect that there was no such person and that my friend had played a trick on me. <break time="0.8s" /> He probably guessed that if I asked about Leonidas, Wheeler would remember a man named Jim Smiley and bore me nearly to death. <break time="0.8s" /> I found Simon Wheeler dozing comfortably by the stove in an old tavern in the mining camp of Angels. <break time="0.8s" /> He was fat and bald, and he had a gentle and simple look on his calm face. <break time="0.8s" /> When I told him the reason why I had come, he backed me into a corner and blocked me there with his chair. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he sat down and began a long story, which he told without smiling once or changing his quiet, gentle voice. <break time="0.8s" /> He seemed to believe that the story was truly important and that its two heroes were men of great genius. <break time="0.8s" /> To me, the funniest thing was the way he told such a silly story so seriously, so I let him go on without interrupting.

There was a man here named Jim Smiley in the winter of 1849, or maybe the spring of 1850, Wheeler began. <break time="0.8s" /> Smiley was the strangest man I ever saw, because he would bet on anything that came up. <break time="0.8s" /> If he could not find anyone to bet on the other side, he would gladly change sides. <break time="0.8s" /> He was lucky, too, so lucky that he almost always came out the winner. <break time="0.8s" /> He bet on horse races and dog fights, and even on which of two birds on a fence would fly first. <break time="0.8s" /> If he saw a bug start to go somewhere, he would bet on how long it would take to get there. <break time="0.8s" /> Once Parson Walkers wife was very sick, and for a long time it seemed that nobody could save her. <break time="0.8s" /> When the parson said she was much better, Smiley answered without thinking, Well, I will bet two and a half dollars she does not get well. <break time="0.8s" /> Smiley also had a slow, sickly old mare, but he used to win money on her all the same. <break time="0.8s" /> Falling far behind at the start, she would get excited near the end and win by a neck.
